lead: Paul says that the things of God can be known only through God’s own Spirit; Jesus tells his disciples to stay awake for a master who will surprise them. Both readings are about being able to recognise the Lord. The Child of Bethlehem was seen by many and recognised by few, and the same is true when he comes again.

r.h: The Spirit that is from God
set: Paul founded the church in Corinth (Acts 18) and writes to it, probably from Ephesus (16:8), about its divisions. Some of the Corinthians prized eloquence and “wisdom”. Paul has answered with the cross. Now he explains how anyone can grasp a wisdom like that: only by the Spirit.
str: v. 11: only a person’s spirit knows that person; only God’s Spirit knows God.
vv. 12–13: we have received that Spirit, and we speak in words he teaches.
vv. 14–15: the unspiritual person and the spiritual person.
kw: Literally “of the soul”: a person living by natural powers alone. It is not a word for a bad person but for someone who has not yet received the Spirit’s light.
A person led by the Holy Spirit. It does not name a special class. Paul soon tells the Corinthians that they are behaving as infants in Christ (3:1).
To sift and judge. It is the key verb of vv. 14–15. Faith has its own way of seeing.
vv: So also no one comprehends what is truly God’s except the Spirit of God.
The comparison runs from the human to the divine: no one can see into my heart from outside. Still less can anyone see into God from outside, unless God gives his own Spirit.
Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may understand the gifts bestowed on us by God.
The Spirit is given so that we may recognise what we have already been given.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 11 in teaching that only the Spirit knows the things of God (CCC 687), and it says that no one can confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Spirit (CCC 683). This gift belongs to all the faithful, who have received the Spirit’s anointing (CCC 91). So v. 15 does not put an individual above the Church’s teaching: Paul writes these words while correcting the very people who thought themselves spiritual.

set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem (9:51). He has just told the disciples not to worry about possessions (12:22–34). He now turns to how they must live while they wait for him.
str: vv. 35–36: dressed and with lamps, like servants waiting for their master.
vv. 37–38: the surprise: the master serves the servants.
vv. 39–40: the thief, and the unexpected hour.
kw: Literally “loins girded”: the long robe tucked into the belt for work or travel. Israel ate the Passover this way, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11).
The same word as in the Beatitudes (6:20–22). The watching slave is a happy person, not an anxious one.
vv: Be dressed for action and have your lamps lit;
Blessed are those slaves whom the master finds alert when he comes; truly I tell you, he will fasten his belt and have them sit down to eat, and he will come and serve them.
No master in that world did this. The roles are reversed, and we see it happen at the Supper: “I am among you as one who serves” (22:27). The one we wait for comes to wait on us.
You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an unexpected hour.
The early Church often used the image of the thief (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 3:3). It is about the timing and nothing else: he comes as a surprise. It says nothing about his character.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, reads the girded loins as self-control and the burning lamps as good works that give light to others (in substance). The Catechism connects watchfulness with prayer: the disciple keeps watch, remembering the first coming in lowliness and hoping for the second in glory (CCC 2612). At this time of the year the Church holds both comings together.

study: Where have I recognised God’s gift only long afterwards? What helped me to see it?
If the Lord comes to serve those who wait for him, how does that change the way I think of waiting?
